review.rationale: The best-grounded candidate remains backend_pool_config_regression (hyp-2354...). It has two independent source types plus a discriminating chronology: changes/config records show runtime-1 applied to backend at 2026-10-11T09:00:27Z (incident_3002-E-003) with db_pool_max reduced 20 -> 2 while backend concurrency remained 155 (incident_3002-E-004); backend metrics show the predicted immediate queueing effect, pool_waiters=153 at exactly 09:00:27Z (incident_3002-E-005); and the downstream gateway 5xx ratio 0.35 follows at 09:00:36Z (incident_3002-E-009), nine seconds after the config change. The backend log 'Request processing exceeded deadline' at 09:00:36Z (incident_3002-E-008) is consistent with request-level deadline failure under queueing, though it is generic and does not itself name pool exhaustion. The competing gateway assets-2 change is explicitly presentation-only with routing unchanged (incident_3002-E-010) and supplies no mechanism; postgres server connections were 30 against connection_limit=100 at 09:00:27Z (incident_3002-E-007), which argues against postgres_connection_exhaustion at that instant but is a single sample. The verdict is still insufficient because the causal mechanism is not directly observed end-to-end: repeated backend metrics queries across the full 08:00-10:00 window, including explicit pool_limit/pool_in_use/pool_available and post-change trend requests, returned only two point-in-time values (request_latency_ms=40 ms at 09:00:00Z and pool_waiters=153 at 09:00:27Z), with no sustained waiters elevation, active-connection plateau at the reduced cap, acquisition errors, or latency rise; the runtime-1 config diff query returned only the db_pool_max/concurrency excerpt (incident_3002-E-004) rather than a complete diff; and all-severity backend logs across the full window returned only the generic deadline line, with a 'pool' keyword search yielding no records. These are blocking causal gaps, not optional corroboration: the config mechanism plus a single matching waiters sample is strong but not sufficient to prove sustained pool starvation under concurrency 155. I therefore request the unobserved causal sources through distinct, previously untried scopes rather than repeating empty telemetry: postgres health metrics (a database channel never queried for this incident) to test the unresolved postgres alternatives, and a targeted redis log/metric check to test the unobserved redis_unavailable alternative. Missing redis/payment telemetry is not treated as refutation of the leading candidate or as support for their hypotheses.
